text: PROMPTER SCRIPT ###PODCAST INTRO Hello and welcome to the Idaho Reports podcast for March 11, I’m Logan Finney. Chronic wasting disease is a fatal neurological condition – a prion like mad cow disease or scrapie – that affects members of the deer and elk family, known as cervids or cervidae. After decades of screening, Idaho’s first CWD case was detected in 2021 outside Riggins, with more positive tests in game animals taken outside New Meadows and Bonners Ferry. In February, the Idaho Conservation League sent a letter to state lawmakers and the Idaho State Department of Agriculture, outlining concerns with documented biosecurity lapses at several domestic elk farms across the state, flagging the possibility of chronic wasting disease transmission between wild and domestic cervids. I sat down with ICL Wildlife Program Associate Jeff Abrams last week to find out more. [INTERVIEW] Idaho State Department of Agriculture Director Chanel Tewalt laid out ISDA’s view of the situation in a letter of her own last F responding to Abrams and ICL’s concerns, which Idaho Reports obtained through a public records request. GFX Tewalt also noted that decisions about what happen to any of the wild animals who interact with domestic herds is the purview of Fish and Game, not the Department of Agriculture. GFX The ISDA letter directly addresses several of ICL’s assertions while leaving the decisions about policy up to lawmakers, adding detail regarding ISDA’s enforcement approach as well as quarantines, testing, and imports at domestic facilities. Chronic wasting disease is a fatal neurological condition – a prion like mad cow disease or scrapie – that affects members of the deer and elk family, known as cervids or cervidae. After decades of screening, Idaho’s first CWD case was detected in 2021 outside Riggins, with more positive tests in game animals taken outside New Meadows and Bonners Ferry. In February, the Idaho Conservation League sent a letter to state lawmakers and the Idaho State Department of Agriculture, outlining concerns with documented biosecurity lapses at several domestic elk farms across the state, flagging the possibility of chronic wasting disease transmission between wild and domestic cervids. I sat down with ICL Wildlife Program Associate Jeff Abrams last week to find out more. [INTERVIEW] Idaho State Department of Agriculture Director Chanel Tewalt laid out ISDA’s view of the situation in a letter of her own last F responding to Abrams and ICL’s concerns, which Idaho Reports obtained through a public records request. GFX: “While extremely unfortunate, CWD exists at endemic levels in other states, and wildlife do not recognize state lines. There is a risk of CWD transmission without domestic cervidae operations having ever existed in Idaho.” Tewalt also noted that decisions about what happen to any of the wild animals who interact with domestic herds is the purview of Fish and Game, not the Department of Agriculture. GFX: “The current IDFG policy is to lethally remove all ingressed wild cervids due to ‘CWD concerns,’ whether the disease has been confirmed on the captive facility or not.” GFX: “Neither of the domestic cervid facilities that experienced recent wild ingresses were under quarantine at the time of the ingress. ISDA agreed to assist IDFG in the cost of managing the ingress as a gesture of good faith to our state partners.” The ISDA letter directly addresses several of ICL’s assertions while leaving the decisions about policy up to lawmakers, adding detail regarding ISDA’s enforcement approach as well as quarantines, testing, and imports at domestic facilities. GFX: “The most recent detection of CWD in a captive elk ranch occurred in Boundary County in an elk herd that has not imported any animals in over a decade.” GFX: “Idaho law does not say that domestic cervidae operations are allowed to exist only if they are perfect. Instead, Idaho law provides for a process to address violations if they occur.” Idaho Reports will continue to cover this story and the spread of Chronic Wasting Disease. ###PODCAST OUTRO While extremely unfortunate, C-W-D exists at endemic levels in other states, and wildlife do not recognize state lines. There is a risk of C-W-D transmission without domestic cervidae operations having ever existed in Idaho. The current Idaho Fish and Game policy is to lethally remove all ingressed wild cervids due to ‘CWD concerns,’ whether the disease has been confirmed on the captive facility or not. Neither of the domestic cervid facilities that experienced recent wild ingresses were under quarantine at the time of the ingress. ISDA agreed to assist IDFG in the cost of managing the ingress as a gesture of good faith to our state partners. The most recent detection of CWD in a captive elk ranch occurred in Boundary County in an elk herd that has not imported any animals in over a decade. Idaho law does not say that domestic cervidae operations are allowed to exist only if they are perfect. Instead, Idaho law provides for a process to address violations if they occur.
